Scuttlebutt
SKUT-ul-but
noun (Silent Generation slang)
Naval, from scuttled butt: a butt is a cask, and a scuttled one has a hole cut in it. The ship’s drinking-water cask, with its opening for the dipper, was the scuttlebutt (recorded from the early 1800s), and sailors gathered there to drink and trade rumors, as office workers later did at the water cooler. The sense of rumor or gossip is recorded from the early 1900s and was universal in the Navy and Marine Corps by the Second World War.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

On a ship, the scuttlebutt was the water cask, and around it the sailors heard everything first: where the ship was going, who was getting promoted, which officer was in trouble. So scuttlebutt came to mean rumor. In the war, scuttlebutt ran wild — the ship was going home, the ship was going to Japan, the war would be over by Christmas. Most of it was wrong. Scripture is sober about rumor. God’s law says, "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" (Lev 19:16), and "Thou shalt not raise a false report" (Exo 23:1). Solomon knew why rumor spreads: "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly" (Pro 18:8) — we like the taste of them. He also knew how to stop it: "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). A Christian does not have to pass on every piece of scuttlebutt; he can let it die at his feet. And the water cask has a better lesson still. Jesus met a woman at a village well, the place where everyone came to draw water and hear the news, and offered her better water than gossip: "the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life" (Joh 4:14). Christ’s words are not rumor but truth, and they never run dry.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (Navy and Marines, from the ship’s water cask; rumor sense from the early 1900s) for rumor and gossip — talebearing Scripture forbids (Lev 19:16), answered by the living water of Christ’s true word (Joh 4:14).

expand to see more

SCUTTLEBUTT, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; Navy and Marine Corps) 1. The ship’s drinking-water cask or fountain. 2. Rumor, gossip. "The scuttlebutt says we’re headed home."

Webster (1828) — SCUTTLE, verb transitive [from the noun.] 1. To cut large holes through the bottom or sides of a ship for any purpose. 2. To sink by making holes through the bottom; as, to scuttle a ship.

Decode for families: scuttlebutt is rumor — let it stop with you unless you know it is true and kind.

Key Scripture

Lev 19:16 — "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people: neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD."

Exo 23:1 — "Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness."

Pro 18:8 — "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly."

Pro 26:20 — "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth."

Joh 4:14 — "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."

Modern Corruption

The word names a real fault plainly: rumor and talebearing, which wound reputations and stir strife whether or not they turn out true.

expand to see more

Much scuttlebutt was harmless guessing about where the ship was bound, and sailors could hardly help wondering. But the word also covered the other kind of talk: who was in trouble, who had done what. Scripture forbids the talebearer (Lev 19:16) and the false report (Exo 23:1), and it knows why such words are tempting (Pro 18:8).

The cure is simple and hard: be the place where the rumor stops (Pro 26:20). A Christian can listen at the water cooler without adding wood to the fire, and can go to the better well for words that are true (Joh 4:14).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Scuttle (to cut a hole) + butt (cask) → scuttled butt (ship’s water cask, early 1800s) → early 1900s Navy (rumor) → WWII universal → everyday gossip.

expand to see more

Scuttle — to cut holes in a ship; a small hatchway

Butt — a large cask for liquids

Early 1800s: scuttlebutt — the ship’s water cask with a hole for the dipper

Early 1900s Navy: scuttlebutt — rumor traded at the cask

1940s–: universal Navy and Marine word; later, any gossip

Usage

""Grandpa says the scuttlebutt on his ship had them going home every week for two years.""

"Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth (Pro 26:20)."

"Thou shalt not raise a false report (Exo 23:1)."
